questions.prompt: What is the built-in potential of a junction with \(N_A = N_D = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)? (\(\varphi_{bi} = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_AN_D}{n_i^2}\), \(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))

questions.prompt: The two ends of a PN junction (\(\varphi_{bi} = 0.8\ \mathrm{V}\)) are shorted with a copper wire. In equilibrium, what current flows, and why?
options: 0.8 V divided by the wire resistance
None: the copper–P and copper–N contacts have contact potentials that exactly cancel φbi around the loop
A small leakage current, IS
A large current at first that slowly decays as the junction discharges
questions.explanation:
KVL around the loop: \(\varphi_{bi} + \varphi_{mn} - \varphi_{mp} = 0\) (reader Eq. 5.45, 5.50). Every junction of dissimilar materials, including metal–semiconductor, forms a contact potential. In equilibrium the sum around any closed loop is zero, otherwise you could extract energy from nothing.
There's no 'charge' to run down; the junction never stored usable energy.

questions.prompt: An ideal voltmeter is connected across an isolated PN junction in equilibrium (\(\varphi_{bi} = 0.7\ \mathrm{V}\)). What does it read?
options: 0 V
It depends on the meter's probe metal
questions.explanation:
The meter's probes make metal contacts on each side, and their contact potentials cancel the built-in potential, just like a shorting wire. The meter measures the difference in electrochemical potential, which is zero in equilibrium.
\(\varphi_{bi}\) is real (it has a field and stored charge), but you can't measure it with a voltmeter. The probe metal doesn't matter: all the contact potentials in the loop cancel.

questions.prompt: The reader models a metal as extremely heavily doped n-type silicon, \(N_m \approx 10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Using \(\varphi = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{n}{n_i}\) for n-type and \(\varphi = -\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{p}{n_i}\) for p-type, find the contact potential between such a metal and p-type silicon with \(N_A = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\): \(\varphi_{mp} = \varphi_m - \varphi_p\).
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_m = 0.026\ln(10^{12}) = 0.718\ \mathrm{V}, \quad \varphi_p = -0.026\ln(10^{6}) = -0.359\ \mathrm{V}\]
\[\varphi_{mp} = 0.026\ln\frac{N_mN_A}{n_i^2} = 0.026\ln(10^{18}) \approx 1.08\ \mathrm{V}\]
Note: reader Eq. 5.46–5.47 write these potentials as \(\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_D}{N_A}\) and \(\frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_m}{N_A}\). That's a typo: with the p-region as reference, the correct form has \(N_DN_A/n_i^2\). The cancellation argument in Eq. 5.48–5.50 still works either way.

questions.prompt: Same model (metal = \(10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) n-type). What is the contact potential between the metal and n-type silicon with \(N_D = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(\varphi_{mn} = \varphi_m - \varphi_n\)?
questions.explanation:
Both are n-type, so the \(n_i\) cancels:
\[\varphi_{mn} = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_m}{N_D} = 0.026\ln(10^{5}) \approx 0.299\ \mathrm{V}\]
Heavier doping in the silicon gives a smaller step to the metal. That is one reason ohmic contacts are made through heavily doped (n⁺/p⁺) regions.

questions.prompt: Why can't a PN junction in thermal equilibrium be used as a battery to power a resistor?
options: Its internal resistance is too high
The built-in field is too weak to drive current
It can, but only until the depletion region discharges
In equilibrium no net energy can flow; the contact potentials around any external loop cancel φbi exactly, so the loop's net EMF is zero
questions.explanation:
The reader compares this to a 'perfect ratchet': if a junction could drive current using only thermal energy at one temperature, it would be a perpetual-motion machine (Sec. 5.4.7).
Providing a metal path just gives carriers another route across the same barrier, and it presents an equal barrier. With an energy input (light, a temperature difference, an applied voltage), the junction can deliver power: that's a solar cell.

questions.prompt: One student computes potentials relative to intrinsic silicon; another uses the P region as the zero. Do they get different built-in potentials for the junction?
options: Yes; the intrinsic reference gives the larger value
Yes; only the P-region reference gives the physical value
No: φbi is a potential DIFFERENCE, so it is the same for any choice of reference
They differ by the contact potential of the metal
questions.explanation:
Moving the zero shifts every potential by the same constant, so differences don't change. \(\varphi_{bi} = \varphi_n - \varphi_p = \frac{kT}{q}\ln\frac{N_DN_A}{n_i^2}\) either way.
Gotcha: the reader switches references between Sec. 5.3 (intrinsic) and Sec. 5.4.7 (P region), and that can look like a different result. It isn't.

questions.prompt: Junction A has \(N_A = 10^{18}\) and \(N_D = 10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Junction B has \(N_A = N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What is \(\varphi_{bi}\) of junction A? (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_{bi,A} = 0.026\ln\frac{10^{18}\cdot10^{14}}{10^{20}} = 0.026\ln(10^{12}) \approx 0.718\ \mathrm{V}\]
Gotcha: exactly the same as junction B. Only the PRODUCT \(N_AN_D\) matters. A very lopsided junction isn't automatically 'stronger'. (Their depletion widths do differ a lot.)

questions.prompt: Which statement about contact potentials is correct?
options: Only PN junctions have contact potentials; metals are equipotential
Every junction of dissimilar materials (P–N, metal–semiconductor, even metal–metal) has a contact potential, and in equilibrium they sum to zero around any closed loop
An ohmic contact has no contact potential
Contact potentials add up around a loop, which is how thermocouples work at a single temperature
questions.explanation:
Reader Sec. 5.4.7: 'the contact between two dissimilar metals creates a potential difference' (set by the work-function difference). An 'ohmic' contact still has a contact potential; it is engineered not to RECTIFY (not to act like a diode).
Gotcha: thermocouples need two DIFFERENT temperatures. At a single temperature (equilibrium) the potentials around a loop always cancel.

questions.prompt: Preview of the MOS capacitor: a heavily doped n⁺ polysilicon gate sits at about \(+550\ \mathrm{mV}\) relative to intrinsic silicon. It is placed over a p-type body with \(N_A = 5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). What is the built-in potential between gate and body, \(\varphi_{gate} - \varphi_p\)? (\(kT/q = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\))
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_p = -0.026\ln\frac{5\times10^{16}}{10^{10}} = -0.026\times15.42 = -0.401\ \mathrm{V}\]
\[\varphi_{bi} = 0.55 - (-0.401) \approx 0.951\ \mathrm{V}\]
This matches the reader's MOS example (about 0.95 V). Even with the gate shorted to the body, this potential appears across the oxide and the body surface. The MOS-structure skill picks it up from here.

questions.prompt: Preview of reverse bias: a junction with \(N_A = N_D = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) (\(\varphi_{bi} = 0.838\ \mathrm{V}\)) has 2 V applied with the N side positive. The contact potentials still cancel each other, so the applied voltage appears across the junction itself. What is the total potential step across the depletion region?
questions.explanation:
KVL: applied voltage plus built-in potential, \(\varphi_{bi} + V_R = 0.838 + 2 = 2.84\ \mathrm{V}\).
No current flows (apart from a tiny leakage), so no voltage drops in the neutral regions or contacts. The depletion region must widen to hold the larger step. That's the reverse-bias skill.

questions.prompt: Preview of the MOS structure: an n⁺-poly gate is shorted to a p-type body by a wire. The oxide is an insulator, so no DC current can flow. Is there an electric field in the oxide?
options: Yes: the gate–body built-in potential (about 1 V) has to appear somewhere in the loop, and it sits across the oxide and the depleted body surface
No: shorting the terminals sets the gate and body at the same potential everywhere
No, because an insulator can't hold a field
Only if a voltage source is added
questions.explanation:
Going around the loop (gate → wire → body contact → body → oxide → gate), the contact potentials of the wire connections and the drops inside the device must sum to zero. The gate and body are different materials with a built-in difference, so a potential drop (and field) ends up across the oxide plus a depleted layer in the body (reader Sec. 7.2.2–7.2.3).
So a MOS capacitor holds charge even at zero applied bias, a key starting point for the MOS skills.
